extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning how to write proofs / anyone learning elementary proof techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Strategies and concrete rules for planning, executing, and writing elementary mathematical proofs (conditionals, negations, quantifiers, contradiction, inference rules, and set-theoretic examples). Geared toward turning scratch-work plans into polished final write-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: To prove a goal of the form P → Q
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume P is true and then prove Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scratch-work form: add P to givens and make Q the new goal. Form of final proof: "Suppose P. [Proof of Q goes here.] Therefore P → Q." Many proof strategies supply the first and last sentences; fill the middle with reasoning that derives Q from P and the givens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove P → Q via contrapositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Because P → Q is equivalent to ¬Q → ¬P, you can prove P → Q by proving ¬Q → ¬P instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scratch-work form: add ¬Q to givens and make ¬P the new goal. Form of final proof: "Suppose ¬Q. [Proof of ¬P goes here.] Therefore P → Q." Example: to prove "If ac < bc then c < 0" show contrapositive "If c > 0 then ac > bc."

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid logical symbols in the final write-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Although logical symbols are useful in scratch work, mathematicians usually try to avoid them in the final write-up and stick to ordinary English as much as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use logical symbols and rules of logic to plan strategy, but write the polished proof in standard English sentences. Using symbols in scratch work is fine; the final proof should read naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: To prove a negated goal ¬P: reexpress or use contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: If possible, reexpress the negated goal as an equivalent positive statement and use other proof strategies; if not, do a proof by contradiction by assuming P and deriving a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reexpressing, use known equivalences (De Morgan, conditional laws, definitions). For contradiction: Scratch-work form transforms goal ¬P into assuming P and deriving a contradiction. Final form: "Suppose P is true. [Proof of contradiction goes here.] Thus P is false."

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction (general advice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the statement to be false and try to reach a contradiction. This gives you an extra assumption to work with but leaves the subgoal vague: produce any impossible conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for contradictions with givens; often if a given has form ¬Q, try to prove Q. The strategy is applicable to any goal when stuck, but try other strategies first if they apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a given of the form ¬P during contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a given ¬P and are doing a proof by contradiction, try making P your goal; proving P contradicts the given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scratch-work: with given ¬P and inner assumption (from contradiction) add goal P. Final proof piece: show P, note contradiction with ¬P, conclude desired result.

rubrics_metrics.name: To use a given of the form P → Q (rules of inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are also given P, or can prove P, then you can conclude Q (modus ponens). If you can prove ¬Q, you can conclude ¬P (modus tollens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for opportunities to add P or ¬Q to your givens list; when either appears use modus ponens or modus tollens immediately. These are rules of inference to add conclusions to the givens column and proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work backward using rules of inference
rubrics_metrics.description: If a given is P → Q and your goal is Q, consider proving P as a subgoal so you can apply modus ponens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform the problem by changing the goal to P; if you can prove P, add one final step to conclude Q. This backward-planning is a common tactic when direct approaches stall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexpress negations and use definitions to discover logical form
rubrics_metrics.description: Write out precise definitions and apply logical equivalences (De Morgan's laws, conditional laws) to rewrite givens or goals into more usable forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: rewrite x ∈ A\B as x ∈ A ∧ x ∉ B, then use De Morgan or conditional equivalences to transform negated statements into conditionals or disjunctions that are easier to use. This often reveals which standard strategy applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving universal statements ∀x P(x)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let x be arbitrary (choose a new variable) and prove P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: x must be a new variable not already used to denote a particular object. Final proof form: "Let x be arbitrary. [Proof of P(x) goes here.] Since x was arbitrary, conclude ∀x P(x)." It is common to omit the explicit phrase and simply start "Suppose P(x)" when x is understood to be arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving existential statements ∃x P(x)
rubrics_metrics.description: Find a specific value of x (a witness) for which P(x) is true, and prove P(x) for that value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a particular x (e.g., solve for x under the assumption P(x)) and start the proof "Let x = (value). [Proof of P(x) goes here.] Thus ∃x P(x)." How you found the witness need not be included in the final proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine strategies for compound goals (e.g., ∀x(P(x) → Q(x)))
rubrics_metrics.description: For goals like ∀x(P(x) → Q(x)), let x be arbitrary, assume P(x), then prove Q(x); combine the universal and conditional strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final proof often begins "Suppose P(x)." You may omit 'Let x be arbitrary' in polished write-ups. Multiple summing-up sentences may be condensed or omitted if readers can fill them in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scratch-work (givens/goal lists) and plan beginning/end sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze logical form, rewrite givens/goals (add assumptions or contrapositives) in scratch work to produce a simpler intermediate problem; the proof technique often supplies beginning/end sentences to connect the revised problem to the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the pattern: rewrite givens and goal in scratch work, note what will be known/assumed after using the strategy, fill in middle reasoning, then write the final proof starting with the strategy's initial sentence(s) and ending with the concluding sentence(s). Revisions can be applied repeatedly to make the problem easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose fresh variable names and avoid hidden assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When introducing an arbitrary object use a variable not already standing for something in the proof; do not assume special properties of an 'arbitrary' variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a letter is already used as a particular object, pick a new one (e.g., y) for arbitraries or witnesses. Treat the arbitrary variable as having no extra assumptions beyond those stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: When stuck, try multiple strategies; practice improves strategy selection
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be more than one strategy for a particular goal form; you may have to try a few before finding one that works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experience to guess which strategy is most likely to work; if stuck, try contraposition, contradiction, reexpressions, rules of inference, or working backward until one yields progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit routine steps in final proofs when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians sometimes skip steps in proofs if knowledgeable readers can be expected to fill them in; summing-up sentences may be condensed or omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write enough detail for the intended audience. If a step is routine for the readership, it can be shortened, but avoid skipping steps that are essential to the logical flow for the intended audience (e.g., beginning students).
